unit.title: Creating content: spreadsheets, formulae and charts

objectives.text: Create a spreadsheet, enter and edit numbers, use spreadsheet tools and formulas to carry out calculations, and create charts with appropriate detail.

lesson.title: Spreadsheets, Formulae and Charts
lesson.summary: Enter and organise numbers in a spreadsheet, use a suitable formula or built-in tool for a calculation, and create a chart that explains the data clearly.

objectives.text: Create a spreadsheet, enter and edit numbers, use spreadsheet tools and formulas to carry out calculations, and create charts with appropriate detail.

sections.heading: Organise data before calculating
sections.body: A spreadsheet stores information in cells arranged in rows and columns. Use clear headings so each number has a known meaning. Enter data carefully, then check it against the original information before calculating. Consistent units and labels reduce mistakes. A well-organised table also makes it easier to sort values, find information and create a useful chart later.

sections.heading: Use formulas and built-in tools
sections.body: A formula tells a spreadsheet how to calculate a result. For example, a total can use a SUM formula or an AutoSum tool. Check which cells are included before accepting the result. If the input changes, a formula can update automatically. This is helpful, but it also means an incorrect cell reference can produce a convincing but wrong answer.

sections.heading: Choose and check a chart
sections.body: A chart can make patterns and comparisons easier to see. Choose a chart type that matches the question, such as a bar chart for categories or a line chart for change over time. Include a meaningful title and labels. Before sharing, compare the chart with the source table to check that the data, scale and selected range are correct.

practice.prompt: A fictional spreadsheet lists monthly volunteer hours in cells B2 to B5. Which formula adds those four cells?
practice.explanation: SUM adds the values in the stated range from B2 through B5.

practice.prompt: Which chart is most suitable for comparing the number of volunteers in four separate fictional teams?
practice.explanation: A bar chart makes it easy to compare totals for separate categories such as teams.

practice.prompt: A spreadsheet formula gives an unexpected total. What should the learner check first?
options: The entered values and cell range used by the formula
Whether to delete the entire sheet
practice.explanation: Checking the data and referenced cells helps identify a likely cause of an unexpected calculation.
